title: Car Washes Are (Finally) Getting What They Deserve…

paras: On February 5th, 2025, one of the biggest car wash chains in America walked into a bankruptcy court in Dallas.
Zips Car Wash had about 260 locations in 23 states.
It owed 654 million dollars.
Twenty days later, Driven Brands, the company behind Take 5, announced it was getting out of car washes completely.
It sold its entire U.S. chain for 385 million dollars.
Then the lawsuits arrived.
California. Arizona. Colorado.
Customers said they paid for one wash and kept getting charged every month.
And in May 2026, the biggest car wash company in the country left the stock market at 7 dollars a share.
Five years earlier, it had sold that same stock to the public for 15.
Here's the strange part.
Americans are paying for more car wash memberships than ever.
The money keeps coming in. The trust doesn't.
This is the story of how washing a car became a subscription, who got rich from it, and why the bill is finally coming due.

sections.chapter: The best idea in car washing
paras: For most of the last century, a car wash was a simple trade.
You pulled in, you paid, you left.
Cash per car.
That changed, quietly, in 2003.
A chain from Tucson, Arizona, called Mister Car Wash launched something it called the Unlimited Wash Club.
One monthly fee. Wash as often as you like.
It sounds like a gift to the customer.
It was really a gift to the business.
A wash that charges per car has good months and bad months, and a rainy weekend can wipe one out.
A wash that charges per month gets paid whether it rains or not.
Private equity noticed.
In 2014, Leonard Green and Partners, a Los Angeles buyout firm, made its first investment in Mister Car Wash.
Seven years later, in June 2021, it took the company public at 15 dollars a share.
On its first day of trading, the stock jumped to 22 dollars and 40 cents.
Wall Street loved one number in particular.
About 1.4 million people were paying Mister every single month.
Those members already made up 62 percent of its wash sales.
That number became the template for an entire industry.
To see why, picture the screen at the pay station.
It's a Saturday morning, and you're behind a line of SUVs.
The screen offers a single wash for around 10 to 15 dollars.
Next to it, in bigger letters, an unlimited plan for about 20 to 25 dollars a month.
That ratio is not an accident.
Industry trade guides say the standard is to price a membership at about two single washes, or less.
Two visits, and it pays for itself.
You tap the plan. So do most of the people in that line.
Now look at it from the other side of the tunnel.
A trade magazine for car wash owners puts the water, power and soap for one car at somewhere between about a dollar thirty and four dollars.
So every visit you make costs the wash a few dollars.
Every month you don't come costs it almost nothing.
Here's the honest part.
We looked for a public number on how often members actually show up.
We couldn't find a reliable one, and Mister Car Wash doesn't put it in its earnings releases.
But we can do rough math with what Mister did publish.
In 2025, it reported just over 1 billion dollars in revenue and about 2.3 million members.
In the last quarter of the year, members made up 79 percent of wash sales.
If roughly three quarters of that revenue came from members, each one paid about 29 dollars a month.
That's a lot of money to wash a car you could rinse in your own driveway.
And it explains the land rush that came next.
Once investors saw monthly billing, car washes stopped looking like a chore and started looking like software with soap.
Private equity firms started buying up local washes and building new ones.
In several recent years, around 900 new car wash locations opened across the country, according to the real estate data firm CoStar.
Most were built on the same plan.
A long tunnel, free vacuums, a bright sign, and a screen that pushes the membership.
And many of them landed on the same roads, fighting for the same drivers.
One trade estimate puts the average wash at about 2,000 members.
Put three new tunnels on one stretch of highway, and someone is going to come up short.
A lot of this was built with borrowed money.
That worked while interest rates sat near zero.
Then they didn't.
Fall number one was the debt.
Zips Car Wash was one of the fastest growers.
Based in Plano, Texas, and backed by the private equity firm Atlantic Street Capital, it reached about 260 locations across 23 states.
When it filed for Chapter 11, it carried 654 million dollars of funded debt.
The plan cut about 279 million dollars of that and handed the company to its private credit lenders.
It also asked to reject the leases on at least 41 locations.
In other words, washes that cost more to keep open than they could bring in.
Zips pointed to competition, rising interest rates and the weight of its debt.
In plain English: too many washes, too much debt, too much rent.
Notice what isn't on that list.
The memberships. They kept billing the whole time.
The court confirmed the plan on April 18th, 2025.
By then, a bigger company had already looked at the same market and decided to leave.
Driven Brands sold nearly 400 U.S. washes to Whistle Express Car Wash for 385 million dollars.
130 million of that wasn't even cash. It was a note, a promise to pay later.
Driven Brands said the sale would help it pay down debt and focus on its oil change business.
Fall number two came from the customers.
Signing up at the screen takes one tap.
Getting out, according to a string of lawsuits, can be a lot harder.
In March 2025, a California man sued GO Car Wash, which runs at least 145 locations in 10 states.
He said he canceled, an employee confirmed it, and he was still charged 34 dollars and 99 cents.
That July, four customers filed a class action against True Blue Car Wash, the owner of Rainstorm and Clean Freak, with more than 70 washes in four states.
They claimed that people who thought they were buying one wash ended up in a monthly plan.
In another California case, a customer suing Soapy Joe's said she didn't notice 25 dollar monthly charges for two months.
To be clear, these are claims in lawsuits, not findings by a court.
But in Colorado, the state itself stepped in.
On August 20th, 2026, the attorney general announced a settlement with Cobblestone Car Wash over its auto-renewal practices.
Cobblestone agreed to pay 1.35 million dollars to about 70,000 customers.
That works out to around 19 dollars each.
It also agreed to give 25 days' notice before raising membership prices.
Nineteen dollars. Less than one month of the plan.
Fall number three was Wall Street.
Remember that 15 dollar IPO?
Mister Car Wash kept growing after it.
In 2025, revenue passed 1 billion dollars for the first time, net income was 103 million, and membership was up 7 percent.
The stock went the other way.
On February 18th, 2026, the company agreed to be taken private by the same firm that took it public, Leonard Green, for 7 dollars a share.
That's less than half the IPO price, and less than a third of that first-day high.
The deal valued the company, including its debt, at about 3.1 billion dollars.
It closed on May 19th, 2026, and the stock stopped trading.
Leonard Green already owned about two thirds of the shares, and funds tied to it had sold shares in the IPO at 15.
Now it was buying the rest back at 7.
Anyone who bought at the IPO and held on lost 53 percent.
Now, the other side, because it matters.
For a lot of drivers, the membership is a good deal.
If you really wash twice a month, a 25 dollar plan beats paying 15 dollars a visit.
And people kept signing up through all of this.
In the first quarter of 2026, Mister's memberships were up 11 percent.
Operators also argue that monthly plans smooth out the weather, keep crews working all year and pay for better equipment.
And on the regulation front, the industry actually caught a break.
The FTC wrote a click to cancel rule that would have made quitting as easy as joining.
On July 8th, 2025, a federal appeals court threw it out on procedural grounds, days before it took effect.
So there's no single federal crackdown.
Instead, the industry is facing state laws and lawsuits, one at a time.
We've seen this story before.
Not at a car wash. At Amazon.
In September 2025, Amazon agreed to pay 2.5 billion dollars to settle FTC claims that it pushed people into Prime and made canceling hard.
One billion in penalties, and 1.5 billion in refunds, up to 51 dollars per customer.
Amazon admitted no wrongdoing.
But the lesson carries over.
When a business earns more from the people who forget than from the people who show up, regulators eventually start counting too.

sections.chapter: So, did they get what they deserve?
paras: So, are car washes finally getting what they deserve?
Some of them are.
The chains that borrowed too much and built too close together paid in bankruptcy court.
The ones accused of trapping customers are paying lawyers, and in Colorado, paying refunds.
And public shareholders of the biggest chain took the loss on the way out.
But the model itself is doing just fine.
Mister went private with roughly 550 locations and the largest car wash subscription program in North America.
And private equity is already talking about a second round.
Here's the number that sums it up.
A plan of about 23 dollars, used twice a month, costs the wash roughly 3 to 8 dollars in water, power and soap.
The rest pays for the land, the debt, and the investors behind them.
The car wash isn't really selling clean cars. It's selling a monthly habit.
And the ones getting what they deserve are mostly the ones who sold that habit with borrowed money.
So next time the screen offers you unlimited, check one thing first.
Count how many times you washed your car last month.
